title: Trump administration weighs ABA law school recognition
excerpt: The Education Department has recommended denying renewal of the ABA’s federal recognition as a law school accreditor. A final decision could come by late December.
body:
The Trump administration is expected to decide by late December whether to keep recognizing the American Bar Association’s law school accrediting arm, a ruling that could accelerate state efforts to build alternatives to ABA approval.

The Education Department has already recommended denying renewal of the ABA’s federal recognition, according to Fox Business. The final decision now rests with Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent. The ABA has held that federally recognized role since 1952.

Fox News reported that losing federal recognition would not automatically end the ABA’s power to accredit law schools or change state bar-admission rules. But it could weaken the group’s long dominance over legal education and push more states to explore other accreditation paths.

“I think the biggest thing is, everyone should know that the federal recognition of the ABA is just the first step,” Adam Biggs, general counsel of the University of Austin, told Fox News Digital. “If they get knocked off their perch, that's going to supercharge the conversations of these state supreme courts to create alternative pathways that are not just the ABA.”

According to Fox Business, the Department of Education said its staff reviewed the ABA’s accreditation standards and found the organization “out of compliance” with federal accreditor regulations. The department did not comment in detail because the process was still moving through review stages, including a September hearing before an advisory committee.

Melissa Hart, the chair of the ABA’s Accreditation Council, said in a statement to Fox News Digital that the council is complying with federal laws and regulations and said the group looked forward to addressing any misconceptions and clarifying the record at its upcoming hearing before the committee. Hart also said, “As a national accrediting body for American law schools, we remain focused on ensuring quality legal education that produces competent, ethical attorneys who are eligible for licensure.”

The Education Department’s staff recommendation follows a process outlined under federal law. Under the Higher Education Act, the education secretary can terminate recognition of an accrediting agency only after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, and accreditors are generally given up to 12 months to come back into compliance before recognition is ended, Fox Business reported.

Fox News also reported that the ABA’s rules have drawn scrutiny from the Justice Department, which has threatened an antitrust investigation over restrictions on adjunct professors teaching core law school courses. In an Oct. 7 letter, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward gave the ABA 15 days to revise or justify its rules, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The ABA has long served as the primary gatekeeper for legal education in the United States. Most states still require graduates to attend an ABA-accredited law school to sit for the bar exam, but that requirement would not disappear automatically if the federal government ends its recognition of the accrediting arm.

Fox News reported that the potential shift could create openings for schools that want to offer cheaper or shorter programs outside the ABA model. One example is a proposed law school at the University of Austin, which Biggs said is considering a two-year track or a combined undergraduate and legal studies model, free tuition and no federal funding.

States are exploring that ground. Fox News reported that state supreme courts generally set their own bar-admission rules, which means graduates of schools approved through alternative state systems could face different paths depending on where they want to practice.

That separation between federal recognition and state licensing is what makes the coming decision significant, as the reporting explains: the administration can affect which accreditor gets federal backing, but it cannot by itself rewrite every state’s bar rules.

title: Keep the Evacuation Orders in Place
excerpt: Orange County should hold evacuation orders until firefighters secure the Norte Fire line, not until pressure to reopen neighborhoods grows.
body:
Orange County should not rush people back into neighborhoods that the Norte Fire is still threatening. When a fire has burned 570 acres, damaged or destroyed six homes, and injured two firefighters, the priority is not convenience. It is containment.

The facts in South Orange County point in one direction. The fire started near Portico Del Norte in the San Clemente area and raced through residential streets in both San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano. By Saturday morning, officials said it was only 5% contained after reaching 465 acres within about three hours. That is not the moment to soften evacuation orders because people want to check on property or return to routine.

The Orange County Fire Authority has already done the hard part by moving quickly, calling in additional strike teams, and using ground crews and water-dropping aircraft. Battalion Chief Mike Yeun said the goal was to keep the fire inside its current footprint, knock down hot spots, and raise containment before residents could return. That is the correct standard. A fire that is still active, still dangerous, and still being fought overnight should not be treated like a completed incident.

The strongest argument for reopening sooner is easy to understand. People want to get back to their homes, gather belongings, care for pets, and see what is left. Quentin Ortega’s experience showed how abruptly the evacuation hit ordinary life. He learned at work that his home was under evacuation, could not get back because roads were blocked, and ended up at a shelter for water and a meal. That kind of disruption is real, and officials should not dismiss it.

But hardship does not change the weather or the fire behavior. Strong Santa Ana winds, heat, and dry brush helped drive the spread, and officials said red flag conditions were set to continue through Saturday evening for much of Los Angeles and Ventura counties. Those conditions matter more than impatience. If a fire has already moved fast through a zone that includes about 4,600 homes, then the cost of a premature return could be another evacuation, more damage, or worse.

The county also needs to treat the shelter system as part of the response, not as an afterthought. Officials said two evacuation centers were open in San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente, with an overnight shelter at the Boys and Girls Club in San Juan Capistrano. They also said the shelters would accept small pets, while nearby animal facilities took in pets. That is how government should behave in a real emergency: keep people together, keep pets accounted for, and make sure the basics are covered while firefighters work.

Steve Concialdi said firefighters had saved thousands of homes in the area. That is an important achievement, but it is also a reason for restraint. Those homes were saved because crews stayed on task while the fire was still moving and the line was still being built. The county should back that effort with patience, road closures, and full support for crews until the line holds.

The right call now is simple: keep the evacuation orders in place for San Juan Capistrano zones four, five, and ten, and San Clemente zones 12 and 13 until firefighters say the area is secure. The fire has not earned an early return, and the county should not gamble with what remains.

title: California braces as El Niño grows more intense
excerpt: Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency on September 21 to speed up El Niño preparations before winter storms and flooding.
body:
California officials are stepping up preparations as El Niño continues to strengthen, with Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office saying the pattern could become the strongest in recorded history.

Newsom declared a state of emergency on September 21 to speed up planning and resource staging ahead of winter storms, coastal flooding and other impacts, according to the governor’s office. The order directs state agencies to protect vulnerable communities, prepare roads and critical infrastructure, stage emergency supplies and help local partners reduce flood, landslide and coastal risks.

The governor’s office said the emerging event is already breaking records and could keep intensifying. The office said a study published in Science last month found El Niño events are now more than 36% stronger than before the industrial era, with the trend accelerating over the last 40 years as the planet warms.

Officials have also pointed to the possibility of heavy rain, flooding, landslides and coastal flooding. The governor’s office said the emergency proclamation allows state agencies to lead flood-risk-reduction work, stage sandbags and pumps, pre-position other equipment and prepare the California National Guard for flood response, search-and-rescue, engineering and logistics missions if needed.

Cal OES Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs said the state is acting before storms arrive. “We are not waiting for this season’s storms to be on our doorstep,” she said in a statement provided by the governor’s office. “Cal OES is leading California’s statewide efforts by bringing state and local partners together, conducting advance planning efforts, and identifying potential needs before impacts occur.”

The warning is landing as Southern California communities are already dealing with coastal damage. The New York Post reported that Long Beach leaders on Friday outlined a recovery plan after powerful surf from Tropical Storm Rachel tore apart homes and infrastructure on the Peninsula. The New York Post said seven homes remain red-tagged, down from eight, and that officials still do not know how many may have to be demolished.

A Los Angeles Times report published September 22 said officials across Southern California were working to shore up hillsides and flood-control systems before the rains begin. The newspaper said forecasters gave this latest El Niño a 75% chance of being stronger than any other since 1950 and a 98% chance of being “very strong” for the three-month period ending in December, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center.

The New York Post also quoted Mayor Rex Richardson as saying, “We’re now shifting into preparing for the next storm while we recover from the impacts of Rachel.” For now, state officials say the goal is to move early, stage resources and reduce the damage before the worst weather arrives.
